opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate two things people often mix together. One is the agent getting better *within* a task: it tries something, the environment pushes back, it reads the error, adjusts, and eventually succeeds. That's really in-context adaptation. It looks like learning, but once the session ends, most of it is gone. The other is the agent actually becoming a better agent over time, carrying what it figured out into the next task. That second kind is what I'd call real self-learning, and we're still pretty early on it.

For that to happen, I think you need three ingredients working together.

First, the agent has to be in an environment that gives it honest feedback. Code that compiles or doesn't, tests that pass or fail, a user who accepts the result or redoes it. Without a reliable signal, the agent is just reinforcing its own guesses, which can make it more confident without making it more correct.

Second, it needs some way to turn experience into something durable. Today that's often memory: notes, skills, reusable procedures it writes down for itself. That's useful and cheap, but it's fairly shallow. The deeper version is when those trajectories, the successes and especially the recovered failures, flow back into training, so the improvement ends up in the weights rather than in a text file. I think the most interesting work right now is figuring out how to close that loop continuously instead of in big, infrequent training runs.

Third, and this is the part I find most underrated, the agent has to be able to judge its own work. If it can verify whether it actually solved the problem, notice where it was uncertain, and decide what's worth trying again, then it can generate its own curriculum. That's when it starts to feel like self-learning rather than just being trained.

So my view is that it doesn't happen through one breakthrough. It happens when good environments, durable memory, and reliable self-evaluation start reinforcing each other. When they do, every task the agent finishes also becomes training data for the next one. That flywheel is what everyone is trying to get spinning.

r001.rationale: The response describes feedback, durable memory or training, and self-evaluation as ingredients, but does not identify advancing the model and agent architecture in sync as a highly likely pathway.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that today it mostly doesn't happen the way people imagine. When we say "self-learning," there's this picture of a model sitting in the world, trying things, and quietly getting smarter on its own. What actually happens right now is much more mediated by humans than that.

The way I'd break it down is into three layers. The first is the weights. For the model to genuinely learn in the deep sense, something has to change in the parameters, and today that only happens in training, driven by reinforcement learning with environments and reward signals that people designed. The agent doesn't choose its own curriculum. We choose what tasks it sees, what counts as success, and how much signal it gets back.

The second layer is context and memory. An agent can "learn" within a session or across sessions by writing things down, retrieving them, and conditioning on them. This looks like learning from the outside, and it's useful, but it's closer to taking notes than to acquiring a skill. If you wipe the notes, the capability is gone.

The third layer, and this is where I think it gets interesting, is the loop between those two. The real question for self-learning is whether an agent can generate its own experience, judge the quality of that experience well enough to turn it into a training signal, and then feed that back into the weights without a human in the middle of every step. The bottleneck isn't compute or data volume. It's verification. In domains like code and math, you have a reasonably reliable signal, so you see fast progress. In open-ended domains, the agent's judgment of its own work is the weakest link, and if you train on that, you amplify its blind spots.

So my view is that self-learning will arrive unevenly. It's already real where the environment can tell you if you're right. It's much further away where the environment can't, and there I think humans stay in the loop longer than most people expect, not because of caution, but because we're still the best reward model available.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop that could update model weights using agent-generated experience, but it does not identify advancing the model and agent architecture in sync as a highly likely pathway.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether an agent can turn experience into a lasting improvement in how it acts. You can give it memory, let it reflect, and let it try again, but that alone doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned.

Imagine an agent working on a coding task. It makes a change, runs the tests, sees a failure, and revises its approach. That’s a feedback loop. The deeper question is: when it encounters a similar problem later, does it avoid the same mistake? Can it apply what it discovered to a different problem?

That improvement might come through updating the model’s parameters, but it could also come through retaining useful knowledge or developing reusable procedures. What matters is that the experience changes its future behavior in a way that generalizes.

And I think the hardest part is the learning signal. An agent can generate a very convincing explanation of why it failed, but that explanation may be wrong. So it needs feedback grounded in something it can check. Otherwise, it risks reinforcing its own misconceptions. For me, self-learning is really that whole loop: act, observe, extract something useful, and verify that it actually helps next time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions model parameter updates and reusable procedures as possible ways to improve, but does not identify advancing the model and agent architecture together as a likely pathway.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether an agent can turn experience into a lasting improvement. Completing a task once doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned anything. The question is: when it encounters a similar problem again, does it make a better decision?

For that to happen, it needs a loop: act, observe the result, identify what went wrong, and carry that lesson forward. That lesson might live in memory, in an updated procedure, or eventually in the model’s parameters. Those are different mechanisms, but they serve the same purpose: changing future behavior based on experience.

The difficult part is the feedback. If an agent judges its own work only by whether the answer sounds reasonable, it can reinforce its own mistakes. It needs something that pushes back—a test result, an observable outcome, or human feedback. And it needs to distinguish a lesson that generalizes from something that happened to work once.

So I’d look less at how much an agent reflects and more at whether its improvements persist and transfer to new situations. That’s where self-learning becomes meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through feedback and changes to memory, procedures, or model parameters, but does not identify advancing the model and agent architecture together as a likely pathway.
